segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, generous, occasionally heated conversation about one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through Charles Dickens' great fog-bound masterpiece — chapter by chapter, character by character, obsession by obsession.
Bleak House was published in monthly instalments between 1852 and 1853, and it has never really gone out of print, or out of relevance.
To help us make sense of it — and to make the making-sense feel like a pleasure — I have three extraordinary companions.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive, and he brings to this table the ear of a performer — the rhythms, the timing, the sheer theatrical delight of the prose.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows Victorian institutions from the inside out — what Chancery actually was, how the courts worked, who they crushed.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times — she reads with the exact combination of love and rigour this novel demands.
Today we're starting at the very beginning — with the fog.
That extraordinary opening, where Dickens doesn't give us a character or a plot — he gives us weather, mud, and the suffocating machinery of the Court of Chancery.
Oliver, you've read that opening aloud more times than most people have read it silently — where does it begin to work on you?
It begins to work before you've fully understood what's happening — which is the trick, isn't it.
Dickens opens Chapter One without a single human being in the frame.
You get London, you get November, you get mud — and then you get that fog.
And the prose does something almost physical — it accumulates, it presses down, it refuses to let the light in.
The sentence I always feel in my chest is this one — Dickens at his most incantatory.
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
That repetition — fog, fog, fog — it's a drumbeat before the story has even started.
When I read it aloud the first time, I realised Dickens wasn't describing a setting — he was composing a piece of music.
That's exactly the word — music.
Because when I first read it — I was sixteen, I had no idea what Chancery was — I didn't understand the legal satire, but I felt it.
The fog gets into you as a reader the way it gets into London — gradually, completely, without asking permission.
And what strikes me now, re-reading, is how precise Dickens is about what the fog conceals.
He writes — and this is a sentence I've turned over many times —

"The raw afternoon is rawest, and the dense fog is densest, and the muddy streets are muddiest, near that leaden-headed old obstruction, appropriate ornament for the threshold of a leaden-headed old corporation: Temple Bar."
That word — leaden.
Heavy with lead, yes — but also leadenly slow, leadenly indifferent.
The fog isn't just weather — it's the moral atmosphere of everything the novel is about to accuse.
And the accusation is very specific — which is easy to miss if you don't know what you're standing in front of.
When Dickens places his fog at the heart of Chancery, he is locating it at an institution that was, by the 1850s, genuinely notorious.
The Court of Chancery handled equity cases — wills, trusts, inheritances — and some of those cases had been running for generations.
There was a real case — Jennens v Jennens — that had been grinding through Chancery for over a century when Dickens was writing.
The estate was worth millions; when the case finally concluded, the costs had consumed nearly everything.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce was not a grotesque exaggeration — it was barely a heightening of what people already knew to be true.
And Dickens says as much, in that magnificent deadpan — let me find the line —
"Jarndyce and Jarndyce drones on. This scarecrow of a suit has, in course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means."
"Scarecrow of a suit" — three words, and you know everything you need to know about how Dickens regards this institution.
"Scarecrow of a suit" — I mean, that is just perfect.
It's something that was once a living thing — a genuine legal dispute between real people — and now it's just rags on a pole, frightening anyone who gets too close.
And what Dickens understood, as a performer understands, is that you can't lecture people into outrage.
You have to make them laugh first — get them leaning in — and then you let them feel the horror underneath.
The fog does that.
It seduces you with its beauty before you realise you can no longer see your hand in front of your face.
There's something else in that fog, though — something that I think is easy to overlook when we're caught up in the satire.
The fog is also Esther's fog — the unknown origins, the hidden past, the mother she doesn't know she has.
From the very first pages, Dickens is setting up two kinds of concealment — the systemic fog of Chancery, and the intimate fog of Esther's identity.
And Esther herself — her narration — is so careful, so self-effacing.
She says, near the start of her first chapter — and this is the line that breaks my heart every single time —
"I have a great deal of difficulty in beginning to write my portion of these pages, for I know I am not clever."
She has been told, her whole life, that she is not clever — that she is less, that she is secret, that she is shame.
And Dickens has the audacity to make that self-doubting woman one of the most capable narrators in Victorian fiction.
The dual narrative structure is worth pausing on, because it's doing real argumentative work.
You have the omniscient narrator — sardonic, furious, in the present tense, firing from a great height.
And then you have Esther — personal, retrospective, humble almost to a fault.
The system view and the human view, side by side — Chancery as abstraction, and then Chancery as it actually lands on a person's life.
That is Dickens' central argument, dressed up as a novel.
And it's an argument that begins, really, in that single word — fog.
Before there's a plot, before there's a character we can follow, there is this pervasive, democratic, absolutely unignorable atmosphere.

In our next segment, we're going to follow that fog down into Chancery itself — the case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce, what it is, what it does to people, and why Dickens chose the law as his great villain.
Stay with us.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great sprawling masterpiece apart — chapter by chapter, character by character, sentence by sentence.
I'm your host, and today we're diving into one of the novel's most sustained and devastating preoccupations: the Court of Chancery, and what it does to everyone it touches.
To help me unpack it, I have three extraordinary guides to this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — he hears the music of this prose the way a conductor hears a score.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian specialising in Victorian institutions — he knows what Chancery actually was, and what it actually cost.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times — she brings the reader's eye, the reader's heart.
Let's begin where Dickens begins — in the fog.
You know, every time I sit down to record the opening chapter of Bleak House, I have to remind myself to breathe.
Because Dickens doesn't give you a sentence — he gives you a weather system.
That opening is one of the great rhetorical performances in the English novel.
He sets up the fog, and then — quite deliberately — he sets up Chancery as the same thing.
The famous passage begins something like this — he reaches into the fog and pulls out the court.
"Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition of this High Court of Chancery."
He is not describing the court — he is diagnosing it.
And performing that line, you feel it in the chest — that word 'floundering' is doing extraordinary work.
And it was a diagnosis that a great many of Dickens' contemporaries recognised as accurate, which is what gave the novel its immediate force.
The Court of Chancery, by the 1850s, was a byword for institutional paralysis.
Cases had been running for decades — some for generations.
There was a real case, Jennens v. Jennens, that had been grinding through the courts for nearly a century, and is thought to be one of Dickens' inspirations for Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
What Dickens understood, with that satirist's precision, is that Chancery wasn't merely slow — it was structurally incapable of resolution.
The costs consumed the estate.
That's not a flaw in the system — by the time Dickens was writing, it was effectively the system.
What strikes me every time I re-read the opening is how Dickens refuses to let you be comfortable about where you are.
The fog isn't just atmosphere — it's epistemological.
You can't see clearly because the court doesn't want you to see clearly.
And then he gives you that remarkable list — all the people ruined or destroyed by Jarndyce and Jarndyce.

"Shirking and sharking, in all their many varieties, have been sown broadcast by the ill-fated cause; and even those who have contemplated its history from the outermost circle of such evil, have been insensibly tempted into a loose way of letting bad things alone to take their own bad course."
That word 'insensibly' — that's the most frightening word in the sentence.
The corruption doesn't announce itself.
It seeps.
Oliver, you've read this novel aloud more times than you can count — do the class dimensions of Chancery become more visible in performance?
Because it strikes me that Dickens populates the court's orbit with people from every rung of the social ladder — but they don't all suffer equally.
Oh, absolutely — and it becomes very clear the moment you give voice to someone like Richard Carstone, as opposed to, say, Mr. Tulkinghorn.
Richard is consumed by Chancery from the inside out — it hollows him, it becomes his whole identity.
Tulkinghorn feeds on it the way a very particular kind of man feeds on other people's secrets.

There's that magnificent exchange where Richard insists the case must come right in the end, and John Jarndyce — who has spent a lifetime watching it not come right — says something almost unbearable.
"It's in the nature of Chancery proceedings to be slow" — but the way Jarndyce says it, it isn't an explanation, it's an elegy.
And the class dimension you're pointing to — Richard has hope because he's young and genteel and believes institutions repay faith.
Jo the crossing-sweeper has no such illusions, because no institution has ever offered him anything but the back of its hand.
That contrast between Richard and Jo is the novel's great structural argument, and I don't think Dickens ever made it more sharply anywhere else in his work.
Richard is destroyed by a system he was taught to trust.
Jo is destroyed by a system that was never designed to notice him at all.
And historically, that's precisely accurate.
Chancery was a court of equity, which in theory existed to provide justice where common law failed.
But equity required property.
Without a stake in the contested estate, you simply didn't exist in Chancery's eyes.
Dickens' genius is to show us the court's shadow falling on people who aren't even party to the suit — the Jellyby children, Gridley, poor mad Miss Flite with her caged birds.
Miss Flite — now there's a character I find both funny and unbearable in equal measure.
She's attended the court every day for years, waiting for judgment.
And her birds — she names them.
She tells Esther that she intends to release them on the day judgment is given — which, of course, means she will never release them.
The names she gives them — Hope, Joy, Youth, Peace, Rest — and then the darker ones: Waste, Want, Ruin, Despair, Madness.
"That's the whole history of Chancery," I always want to say — and Dickens knows it.
The trajectory from Hope to Madness is the trajectory of every character Chancery gets its hands on.
It's one of the most compressed, elegant structural symbols in Victorian fiction.
James, I want to push on something — because Dickens is clearly furious about Chancery, but he's also furious about something broader, isn't he?
The court seems to stand in for a whole philosophy of how English society orders itself.
Yes — and this is where I think the novel rewards careful historical attention, because Dickens is making an argument that goes well beyond legal reform.
Chancery is a metonym for what we might call the apparatus of aristocratic self-perpetuation — the web of deference, precedent, and mystification that keeps power exactly where it is.
Look at Tulkinghorn — he has no title, no estate.
He is entirely made of secrets about the aristocracy.
His power derives entirely from their dependence on his silence.
Dickens describes him moving through Chesney Wold — that extraordinary image of him as a piece of old furniture in the landscape of the great house.
"He is of no use in the aspect of those old buildings; but he is in possession of their secrets."
That's the symbiosis Dickens is anatomising — the law doesn't serve the class system, it is the class system.
And Tulkinghorn is such a pleasure to perform precisely because he is so utterly withholding.
Most Dickens characters telegraph their inner life — Tulkinghorn gives you nothing.
Dickens says of him that he never converses — he listens and advises.
The contrast with someone like Chadband — who is all performance, all hot air and Biblical ventriloquism — couldn't be sharper.
Chadband preys on the poor with language.
Tulkinghorn preys on the powerful with silence.
Between the two of them, Dickens has covered the whole field of how class enforces itself.
I want to come back to what Oliver said about Richard, because I think that's where the novel breaks your heart most efficiently.
Richard is charming and young and has every advantage — except the one that Chancery requires, which is the willingness to give up.
There's a passage late in the novel where Esther visits him, and she sees him utterly wasted by the suit.
"He was not shabby, but he was...pale, and worn, and I grieved to see how young he looked."
It's that last phrase — 'how young he looked' — that undoes me every time.
Youth destroyed.
And what's insidious is that Chancery didn't do it with malice — it did it with sheer indifference.
That word — indifference — feels like the key to the whole thing, doesn't it?
Not cruelty, but the structural absence of care.
Oliver, James, Caroline — there's so much more to explore here, and we'll be back after a short break to look at what Dickens proposes — if anything — as an alternative to the world Chancery creates.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time in the fog of Chancery, in the brickmaker's cottage, in Chesney Wold.
Now we turn to the character who may be Dickens' most heartbreaking study in wasted potential: Richard Carstone.
Richard begins the novel as everything a young man should be — charming, warm, genuinely gifted.
And he ends it destroyed — not by villainy, not by accident, but by a lawsuit and his own susceptible nature.
Caroline, you've called Richard one of the most devastating portraits in Victorian fiction.
Where does that tragedy begin for you?
It begins almost the moment we meet him, which is the cruelty of it.
He arrives at Bleak House in those early chapters — young, laughing, trying out every profession in his imagination before breakfast.
Esther notices it with affection at first.
But Jarndyce sees it more clearly from the start — that restlessness isn't just youthful energy.
There's a passage where Esther reflects on his tendency to take up things with great ardour and then let them fall.
Dickens gives us something like: 'He had great freshness and enthusiasm — but no sustained purpose.'
That phrase — 'no sustained purpose' — is the novel's quiet verdict on Richard, and it's delivered so early.
We know what's coming before he does.
And Dickens makes it so pleasurable to watch at first — that's the trap he sets for the reader.
The surgeon phase, the law phase, the army phase — Richard trying each one on like a coat at a tailor's.
There's genuine comedy in it.
Dickens loved performing that kind of character in his readings — the young man of infinite promise and no follow-through.
But then Chancery gets its hooks in.
Jarndyce tries to warn him — one of the great warning speeches in the novel.
'Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here,' he tells him.
And Richard smiles, and nods, and absolutely does not listen — because he can't.
The suit is already in his blood.
That warning from Jarndyce is crucial, and historically it's almost a documentary quotation.
Every Victorian who had dealings with the Court of Chancery knew that warning — it was proverbial.
Cases ran for decades.
The real case of Jennens v Jennens, which Dickens had in mind, ran from 1798 until after the supposed fortune had been entirely consumed by costs.
So what happens to Richard is not melodrama — it's a structural inevitability for anyone who made the mistake of depending on a Chancery suit.
Dickens understood that the Court didn't need villains — the machinery itself was the villain.
Richard simply gets caught in the gears.
And what's so precise about Dickens' portrait is that Richard meets the suit halfway.
He's not a passive victim — there's a weakness in him that reaches toward the dependency the suit offers.
The lawsuit becomes a substitute for the sustained purpose he can't generate himself.
There's a terrible moment — I think it's in one of the middle numbers — where Esther tries to reach him, and he turns on her.
He accuses Jarndyce of having interests adverse to his own — his dearest friend.
Dickens writes it with such quiet, undemonstrative sadness.
He doesn't editorialise.
He just shows you Richard's face, and Esther's, and leaves the damage visible.
That refusal to editorialise is the mark of the later Dickens, I think.
The early Dickens would have given you a speech.
By Bleak House, he trusts the scene.
And Richard's final chapter — when the verdict comes in, and the estate has been wholly consumed — is almost unbearable to perform.
The moment when he says he can begin the world — he now sees it clear.
'I will begin the world,' he says — and he's dying as he says it.
You get a glimpse of who he might have been, in the very moment he ceases to be.
I've never found a way to read that passage dry-eyed.
There's a particular bitterness in the detail that the costs consumed the estate — that Jarndyce and Jarndyce ends not with resolution but with annihilation.
All the parties who devoted themselves to the suit — Richard above all — receive precisely nothing.
And Dickens is historically accurate: that was exactly how major Chancery suits ended.
The lawyers alone profited.
Vholes — Richard's solicitor — is one of Dickens' finest studies in a certain kind of institutional evil.
He has a family to support, he tells us — three daughters and a father in the Vale of Taunton.
Dickens gives him that humanising detail and somehow makes it worse.
Vholes isn't monstrous — he's merely respectable.
That word — respectable — is doing so much work throughout the novel.
But on Vholes it's a verdict and a condemnation at once.
That description of him in black, the colour of a crow — picking clean.
Dickens writes that Vholes is 'a sallow man with pinched lips, who looked as if he had not been fed enough.'
The implication is that he is being fed — on Richard's hopes.
What I find extraordinary is that Richard trusts him.
That's the novel's portrait of delusion — we trust the people who confirm what we want to believe.
And Ada — Ada watching all of this — is one of the more quietly devastating presences in the book.
She loves him past all sense.
She marries him secretly because she knows — with a terrible clarity — that Jarndyce would try to protect her from the sinking ship.
And she wants to go down with it.
When Esther finally sees them together — Ada holding Richard's child, Richard fading — the prose goes very still.
Dickens gives us: 'He looked at me with a smile, and turning gently to his wife, breathed a long breath.'
A long breath.
Dickens knew exactly what he was doing with those three words.
The whole tragedy exhaled in a single sentence.
The whole tragedy exhaled — that's Richard Carstone in a phrase.
A character who holds such promise and is hollowed out — by the law, yes, but also by something in himself that the law simply found and exploited.
Coming up, we'll stay with the theme of damaged lives and turn to someone who has no ward in Chancery, no guardian, no name.
We're going to talk about Jo.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great sprawling masterpiece apart — slowly, lovingly, and without mercy.
I'm your host, and today we're gathered around one of the novel's most compelling and heartbreaking figures: Lady Dedlock.
She is the great masked face at the centre of the novel — aristocratic, glacial, and concealing a secret that will destroy her.
To help us unpick that mask, I'm joined by three wonderful companions.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced Lady Dedlock in more recorded editions of this novel than he'd probably care to count — he hears her from the inside.
James Blackstone brings the institutional machinery — the Chancery, the class system, the legal trap that makes Lady Dedlock's secret so catastrophically dangerous.
And Caroline Woodcourt has been reading this novel since she was seventeen, and she will tell you, with some feeling, exactly what it does to you.
Oliver — Dickens introduces Lady Dedlock with an almost ceremonial formality, doesn't he?
He does, and it's one of the great theatrical entrances in nineteenth-century fiction.
Dickens doesn't give her to us — he withholds her.
We get Chesney Wold first: the rain, the dripping trees, the ghost's walk.
And then the house, and then the servants gossiping, and only then — Lady Dedlock herself, bored.
Dickens gives us this magnificent opening description of her — her high-bred indifference, what he calls her 'exhausted composure.'
'She is perfectly well-bred. If she could be translated to Heaven tomorrow, she might be expected to ascend without any rapture.'
That is a comic line — but it has a chill running through it.
She is so far inside her performance of aristocratic boredom that Heaven itself wouldn't move her.
And that performance is not purely temperamental — it is structurally required of her.
Lady Dedlock has married into one of the oldest families in England.
Sir Leicester Dedlock is not a bad man — Dickens is careful about that — but he is the living embodiment of a class that has calcified around its own dignity.
For Lady Dedlock, boredom is social armour.
It signals that she is above feeling — and therefore above suspicion.
She comes from obscure origins — Dickens is vague about them, deliberately — and she has had to construct this persona entirely from scratch.
Which makes the mask not just social performance, but survival strategy.
What I find so extraordinary is the moment the mask slips for the very first time.
Tulkinghorn is reading aloud from the Jarndyce documents — and she sees the handwriting.
Nemo's handwriting. The man she loved. The father of her child.
Dickens writes it so quietly — he barely raises his voice.
'My Lady Dedlock has been looking out of window; she turns her head, and asks indifferently, "Who copied that?"'
One question. That's all she allows herself.
And Tulkinghorn — Tulkinghorn notices.
That single lapse of composure sets the entire catastrophe in motion.
And what a villain Tulkinghorn is to have in place at that precise moment.
He's Dickens' most unsettling creation, I think — because he has no motive we can name.
He is not jealous, not in love with her, not after money.
He simply wants to know her secret — and once he knows it, to hold it.
Dickens describes him as one of those who never look up — his gaze always at the ground, always the documents, always the files.
He is the novel's great emblem of power-without-feeling — which is also, come to think of it, what Lady Dedlock performs.
Except hers is a performance and his is simply what he is.
That distinction matters enormously when you think about how the novel handles information and class.
Lady Dedlock's secret is, at its core, a secret about origins — she had a child outside marriage, by a man of lower station.
In the Victorian system, that is not merely a moral failing. It is a legal and social annihilation.
It would end her marriage, strip her of position, expose Sir Leicester to public humiliation.
Dickens understood — and I think he felt — that the Victorian class structure demanded a kind of permanent self-erasure from women who had transgressed.
Lady Dedlock hasn't simply kept a secret. She has abolished her own history.
And Esther doesn't know she's her mother. That's the novel's most piercing irony.
The two narrators of the book — Esther's warm, self-doubting voice and Dickens' cold third-person — are circling around the same secret from opposite directions.
When they finally meet — when Lady Dedlock comes to Esther and confesses — the scene is almost unbearable.
She falls to her knees. This woman who has never been seen to feel anything — she falls to her knees before her daughter.
Dickens writes it with such restraint — which makes it more devastating, not less.
'I am your wicked and unhappy mother. O try to forgive me!'
Five words into that sentence and I am finished every single time.
I've read that scene — out loud, in recording booths, more times than I can count.
And what gets me every time is not the kneeling — it's the word 'wicked.'
She uses the word her aunt used about her. The word she was raised to believe about herself.
She has internalized her own condemnation.
And then she vanishes back into disguise almost immediately — because she has to.
She puts the mask back on. There is something almost heroic about it — and something absolutely shattering.
The novel's end — her end — is the logical completion of that trajectory.
She is found dead at the gate of the pauper's burial ground — the same ground where Nemo is buried.
She has dressed as a brickmaker's wife — stripped herself of every last marker of class.
In death, she abolishes the Lady Dedlock persona entirely.
She goes back to what she was before the mask — which is also, in a sense, what the novel has been doing to her all along.
Dickens could be sentimental about women — he often was — but here he is pitiless and precise.
The system doesn't forgive. And neither, finally, does she forgive herself.
I want to come back to Esther for a moment, because I don't think we can talk about the mask without talking about its mirror.
Esther is disfigured by smallpox partway through the novel — and what does she lose? Her face.
Lady Dedlock lives behind a face that is not hers — a performance of character she does not feel.
Esther loses the face she was given and finds, painfully, the self beneath it.
Mother and daughter. One masked, one unmasked. Both by violence — one social, one physical.
Dickens was doing something very deliberate there — and it rewards every re-reading.
The mask, the mirror, the secret — and always, beneath them, the ghost's walk at Chesney Wold, waiting.
There is something in this novel that insists the past is never past — it will always find you at a gate.
We'll be turning next to the third-person narrator — Dickens' own relentless, sardonic eye — and asking what it means that he gives us so much more than any character knows.
Stay with us.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart sentence by sentence — and puts it back together with fresh eyes.
I'm your host, and each week we dig into a different aspect of this extraordinary book — its legal satire, its social conscience, its extraordinary range of human feeling.
Today we're looking at something that might seem, on first glance, almost paradoxical: the comedy of desperation.
Because Bleak House is, among many other things, a genuinely, hilariously funny novel — and it gets some of its sharpest laughs from people in extremis.
Joining me today are three voices who know this territory intimately.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — he hears the prose the way Dickens heard it, as something to be spoken, performed, inhabited.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian whose work on Victorian institutions gives us the real ground beneath Dickens' satire.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House five times and still finds things on every page that make her stop and read aloud to whoever's nearby.
Welcome, all three of you — and let's start with the obvious question: how does Dickens make desperate people funny without making us feel guilty for laughing?
The guilt is the point, I think — or rather, Dickens engineers the comedy so that the laugh and the wince arrive simultaneously.
Think of old Smallweed — Grandfather Smallweed, propped up in his chair, forever subsiding into a heap and being shaken back into shape by his granddaughter Judy.
It is purely, gloriously slapstick — and yet this man is a usurer who has ground the faces of the poor for decades.
Dickens gives us the image of him being shaken like a bolster — and his own description is rather wonderful.
"Shake me up, Judy. Shake me up!"
And Judy shakes him, and he subsides again, and we laugh — but he's a man who has outlived every human feeling except avarice.
That laughter has teeth.
And the thing is, Dickens trusts you to hold both feelings at once — the hilarity and the horror — without spelling it out.
What I find extraordinary is that the comedy of desperation is also the comedy of people who have no self-awareness about their own desperation.
Mr. Skimpole is the supreme example — a man who professes complete helplessness in the face of the world's practical demands.
He calls himself a child in matters of money — and genuinely seems to believe it.
There's that scene early on where he's about to be arrested for a small debt — and he turns to Jarndyce and to young Esther with perfect serenity.
"I don't mean to say that I have not occasionally been in want of money. I have frequently been in want of it."
And then he simply expects someone else to solve it — with absolute, untroubled confidence.
It's funny and it's monstrous, and Dickens knows exactly which one to foreground in any given moment.
What I'd add is that the desperation in Bleak House isn't metaphorical — it's institutional.
The comedy of Chancery is the comedy of a system that has made human misery into a self-perpetuating mechanism.
Gridley — the Man from Shropshire — is perhaps the most precise instance of this.
He has been ruined by Chancery, and he is furious, and his fury is entirely justified — but from the outside it looks like a man shouting at a fog.
And that is Dickens' mordant joke: the system is so diffuse that there is no one to be angry at.
Gridley himself says something that is both laughable and devastating — in the scene where he faces the Lord Chancellor.
"I have been dragged for five-and-twenty years over burning iron, and I have lost the habit of making myself agreeable."
There's something almost absurdist about it — but Dickens isn't writing absurdism, he's writing documentary satire.
James puts his finger on something crucial: the comedy of desperation in Bleak House is always specific.
Dickens never does generalised misery — there's always a particular, absurd, unforgettable detail.
Take Krook's shop — this chaos of bones and bottles and paper, with Krook himself barely distinguishable from the wreckage around him.
And Krook has taught himself to recognise letters one at a time — but he won't let anyone teach him to read, because he wants to do it his own way.
It's absurd. It's poignant. And it's a perfect metaphor for Chancery itself — accumulating documents it cannot process.
Dickens writes that Krook was called the Lord Chancellor — and his shop, the Court of Chancery.
"Both are alike in being ruinous, both in having mountains of costly nonsense accumulated in them."
Dickens throws that in almost parenthetically — but it's the whole satirical engine of the novel in one sentence.
And what gets me, re-reading that passage, is the tenderness underneath the joke.
Krook is frightening, yes — but he's also lonely, and lost, and surrounded by other people's stories that he can't read.
I think the character who breaks me in this register — where funny and desperate collide most painfully — is actually Miss Flite.
She is, by any clinical description, a woman who has been driven out of her mind by Chancery.
She keeps caged birds and she has named them — Faith, Hope, Charity, Patience, Fortitude — and then the darker ones: Ruin, Despair, Madness.
She says she will release them when the case is settled — and she has been saying this for decades.
She speaks in a kind of cheerful, staccato urgency — and Dickens gives her this wonderful line about the wards in Jarndyce.
"When the case is over. Whichever way it goes. I have a presentiment that it must be over — soon. Ve-ry soon."
That fragmented rhythm — the way she speaks in dashes and pauses — is Dickens writing desperation as syntax.
Miss Flite is, in fact, historically very precise — there were such figures haunting the Courts of Chancery.
People who had been drawn in as young litigants and simply never left — because leaving would mean accepting that the loss was permanent.
The comedy of Miss Flite is the comedy of a person maintaining dignity within a system designed to strip it away.

And Dickens understood — as his own experience with his father's debts and the blacking factory taught him — that there is nothing more human than maintaining a kind of theatrical self-possession in the face of ruin.
That is the Dickensian comedy of desperation, at its core: it is always a performance of survival.
Performance of survival — I'm going to steal that phrase, James.
Because that is precisely what Chadband is doing — performing — even if what he's performing is pomposity rather than poverty.
Chadband is desperate for an audience, desperate for food, desperate for the sound of his own voice.
And his sermons — those magnificent, tumbling, circular sermons — are performances of a man filling a void.
There's the passage where he holds forth to poor Jo — Jo who has nothing, who knows nothing — about what it is to be in a state of Terewth.
"What is peace? Is it war? No. Is it strife? No. It is the one thing needful, it is the ray of light, it is the ray of joy."
It's a parody of evangelical rhetoric — and yet Jo is sitting there, starving, with no idea what any of it means.
The comedy becomes a form of cruelty — but it's the preacher who's cruel, not the novel.
That distinction is so important — the novel never mocks Jo.
Jo is the still point around which all the comic desperation orbits — and he himself has no comedy.
He is just desperately, nakedly, without defence.
And that's what makes the Chadband scene so unbearable to re-read — the grotesque comedy is directly adjacent to a child who is dying.
Dickens knows exactly where the floor is.
That phrase — Dickens knows exactly where the floor is — might be the best summary of what we've been circling today.
The comedy of desperation isn't callous — it's calibrated.
Smallweed and Skimpole and Miss Flite and Chadband — each of them funny, each of them a kind of warning, each held in exactly the right light.
Coming up next, we'll turn to the novel's other great engine — the mystery plot, and what Dickens actually does with secrets.
Stay with us.
We've spent this episode moving through the labyrinth of Bleak House — the fog, the law, the fever, the long slow damage done to ordinary lives.
Now we reach the end — and Dickens gives us something more complicated than either triumph or tragedy.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce collapses into nothing. Tulkinghorn is dead. Lady Dedlock is found frozen at the gate of the pauper burial ground where her lover lies.
And Esther — our narrator, our survivor — ends up in a second Bleak House, with Allan Woodcourt, quietly content.
Is that redemption? Or is it something more ambivalent? I want to put that question to all three of you.
The question of whether Esther's ending is redemption or just — survival with a nice house — is one I've wrestled with across several recordings.
What I keep landing on is this: Dickens gives Esther the second Bleak House deliberately, as an act of symbolic insistence.
He's saying: the name that was curse and fog and ruin — I am going to remake it into something that breathes.
But the final lines of Esther's narrative are extraordinary. She can't quite complete the sentence about her own face.

She says — and this is the very last thing she writes — 'I know that my dearest little pets are very pretty, and that my darling is very beautiful, and that my husband is very handsome, and that my guardian has the brightest and most benevolent face that ever was seen, and that they can very well do without much beauty in me.'
She cannot say she is beautiful. She stops just short.
That ellipsis — that unfinished claim — is everything about what Dickens could and couldn't give her.
That ending wrecks me every time, and Oliver's put his finger precisely on why.
Esther has spent the entire novel not quite believing she deserves to exist fully — not deserving love, not deserving to take up space.
And even in triumph, even in happiness, she deflects.
What I find so painful — and so honest — is that Dickens doesn't cure her of it. He just surrounds her with people who love her anyway.
Think of Jarndyce releasing her from the engagement. That scene is almost unbearably tender.
He has foreseen her love for Allan Woodcourt and engineered her happiness — not because he doesn't love her, but because he loves her absolutely and selflessly.
Jarndyce is, in some ways, the moral centre of the novel — and he gives himself the quiet dignity of renunciation.
I want to set Esther's ending — moving as it is — against the other ending that Dickens provides: the death of the suit itself.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce is finally heard — and the estate is found to have been entirely consumed by the costs of the litigation.
Richard Carstone — who has given his health, his marriage, his mind to that hope — collapses and dies on the day he learns there is nothing.
Now, Dickens knew very well that this was not a grotesque invention. Chancery suits of sixty, seventy years' standing were a documented reality.
He even prefaced the novel by noting that everything touching the Court of Chancery in these pages is substantially true.
The system didn't ruin people through malice. It ruined them through procedure — through sheer institutional indifference to human time.
Richard is the novel's clearest demonstration that hope, misplaced and institutionally cultivated, is itself a form of destruction.
And Richard's death is devastating precisely because Dickens refuses to make it melodramatic.
He has Richard say, very quietly — and this is one of the great deathbed lines in the whole of Victorian fiction —
'I will begin the world.'
Three words. The world he is about to leave.
Dickens understood that the saddest things are said simply. He'd learned that from the stage — from Lear, from the clowns.
You don't ornament grief. You let the plainness break the heart.
Lady Dedlock's death has an entirely different register — and I think it's the most formally audacious thing Dickens does at the novel's end.
She has fled through the snow, in disguise, in anguish — and she is found by Esther at the gate of the burial ground where Nemo, Captain Hawdon, her lover and Esther's father, lies.
She has dressed in the clothes of Jenny the brickmaker's wife — the woman who once sheltered Esther.
So at the moment of her death, the great lady and the poorest woman in the novel have exchanged places entirely.
Dickens writes that Esther saw a woman lying at the gate — and he says the words with terrible precision:
'I looked at the face and saw my mother, cold and dead.'
No preamble. No softening. Just the fact — and then the full weight of it.
That image — Lady Dedlock in a pauper's clothes at a pauper's gate — is socially precise as well as emotionally devastating.
Tom-All-Alone's — the slum that Chancery has created through decades of contested ownership — becomes the instrument of her death too.
She dies fleeing Bucket and the law that Tulkinghorn set in motion before Tulkinghorn himself was shot.
The machinery of Victorian social shame — the law, the detective, the aristocratic reputation — grinds her down as surely as the institution grinds Richard.
And Dickens, who could be sentimental, refuses sentiment here. He gives her no deathbed speech, no reconciliation with Esther while still conscious.
She is simply — gone. Found. And that is all.
Inspector Bucket is worth a moment here, because he's a figure we haven't fully reckoned with.
He's often called the first detective in the English novel — and he's magnificent. Cheerful, relentless, genuinely fond of Esther.
But he is also the arm of a system that destroys Lady Dedlock. He's the human face of institutional pursuit.
Dickens gives him this marvellous tic — he's always extending his fat forefinger, pointing at the thing he knows, at the person he's watching.
'Mr. Bucket of the Detective,' says Dickens, as if the title were a fact of nature — and in a sense, it is.
He can't help being what he is. That's the sinister warmth of him.
Before we close, I want to come back to Esther — because I think the question of what she receives at the end is genuinely unresolved.
She has love, she has her children, she has a home named after the house that shaped her.
But the scars from her illness remain. She does not entirely recover her old face, and Dickens does not pretend otherwise.
There's a passage where Allan Woodcourt looks at her — and the way Dickens phrases his gaze is everything.
He doesn't say Allan finds her beautiful in spite of the change. He says Allan looks at her the way he always looked — as if there is no difference worth naming.
That is love as Dickens understood it at his best — not sentiment, but recognition. Seeing someone whole.
What I keep returning to, as a closing thought, is the novel's final distribution of what we might call institutional justice.
Chancery is not reformed. The Court still stands. The fog in the first chapter has not lifted — it has simply moved on to destroy other families.
Dickens was writing at the moment when Chancery reform was actually beginning — the Chancery Procedure Acts of the 1850s were changing things incrementally.
But he didn't trust incremental. He didn't trust the institutions to cure themselves. And on that point, history has been rather mixed in its verdict.
Oliver, I want to give you the last word on the novel as a whole — as someone who has voiced it, lived inside it, come back to it again and again.
What does Bleak House leave you with, finally?
What it leaves me with — every time — is the opening paragraph. I always end where Dickens begins.
Because he wrote the fog before he knew exactly where all of it was going — and somehow that fog contains everything that follows.
He writes:
'Fog everywhere. Fog up the river where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping.'
And then — the line that gets me every time, the one I have to breathe before I read it —
'And hard by Temple Bar, in Lincoln's Inn Hall, at the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor in his High Court of Chancery.'
The fog is the system. The system is the fog. That's the whole novel in two sentences.

And yet — and this is the miracle of Dickens — out of that fog come Esther, and Jarndyce, and Jo looking up at the stars, and Bucket with his pointing finger, and the Bagnets having dinner, and Mrs. Jellyby never looking at her children.
The comedy and the grief in the same breath. That's what he could do that no one else could.
The comedy and the grief in the same breath. I don't think we can do better than that.
My thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, to Professor James Blackstone, and to Caroline Woodcourt — three guides through the fog who have made this novel feel new again.
Bleak House was published in 1852 and 1853, in twenty monthly parts. It has never been out of print.
Perhaps because it knows — as Dickens knew — that the fog has not lifted. But also that people find each other in it.
This has been Bleak House Unpacked. Thank you for listening.

course of time, become so complicated that no man alive knows what it
means. The parties to it understand it least, but it has been
observed that no two Chancery lawyers can talk about it for five

premises. Innumerable children have been born into the cause;

suit. The little plaintiff or defendant who was promised a new

other world. Fair wards of court have faded into mothers and
grandmothers; a long procession of Chancellors has come in and gone

bills of mortality; there are not three Jarndyces left upon the earth
perhaps since old Tom Jarndyce in despair blew his brains out at a
coffee-house in Chancery Lane; but Jarndyce and Jarndyce still drags

How many people out of the suit Jarndyce and Jarndyce has stretched
forth its unwholesome hand to spoil and corrupt would be a very wide
question. From the master upon whose impaling files reams of dusty
warrants in Jarndyce and Jarndyce have grimly writhed into many
shapes, down to the copying-clerk in the Six Clerks’ Office who has
copied his tens of thousands of Chancery folio-pages under that
eternal heading, no man’s nature has been made better by it. In
trickery, evasion, procrastination, spoliation, botheration, under
false pretences of all sorts, there are influences that can never
come to good. The very solicitors’ boys who have kept the wretched
suitors at bay, by protesting time out of mind that Mr. Chizzle,
Mizzle, or otherwise was particularly engaged and had appointments
until dinner, may have got an extra moral twist and shuffle into
themselves out of Jarndyce and Jarndyce. The receiver in the cause
has acquired a goodly sum of money by it but has acquired too a
distrust of his own mother and a contempt for his own kind. Chizzle,
Mizzle, and otherwise have lapsed into a habit of vaguely promising
themselves that they will look into that outstanding little matter
and see what can be done for Drizzle—who was not well used—when
Jarndyce and Jarndyce shall be got out of the office. Shirking and
sharking in all their many varieties have been sown broadcast by the
ill-fated cause; and even those who have contemplated its history
from the outermost circle of such evil have been insensibly tempted
into a loose way of letting bad things alone to take their own bad
course, and a loose belief that if the world go wrong it was in some
off-hand manner never meant to go right.

would go out, Sir Thomas Doodle wouldn’t come in, and there being
nobody in Great Britain (to speak of) except Coodle and Doodle, there

national calamity, however, was averted by Lord Coodle’s making the
timely discovery that if in the heat of debate he had said that he
scorned and despised the whole ignoble career of Sir Thomas Doodle,
he had merely meant to say that party differences should never induce
him to withhold from it the tribute of his warmest admiration; while
it as opportunely turned out, on the other hand, that Sir Thomas
Doodle had in his own bosom expressly booked Lord Coodle to go down

been some weeks in the dismal strait of having no pilot (as was well

On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be
sitting here—as here he is—with a foggy glory round his head,
softly fenced in with crimson cloth and curtains, addressed by a
large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an
interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain
and breaks the heart, that there is not an honourable man among its
practitioners who would not give—who does not often give—the
warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come
here!”

knows—or has some reason to know by this time, the matter having
been rather frequently mentioned. My Lady Dedlock, having conquered
HER world, fell not into the melting, but rather into the freezing,
mood. An exhausted composure, a worn-out placidity, an equanimity of

trophies of her victory. She is perfectly well-bred. If she could be

without any rapture.

Sooth to say, they cannot go away too fast, for even here my Lady
Dedlock has been bored to death. Concert, assembly, opera, theatre,
drive, nothing is new to my Lady under the worn-out heavens. Only
last Sunday, when poor wretches were gay—within the walls playing
with children among the clipped trees and the statues in the Palace
Garden; walking, a score abreast, in the Elysian Fields, made more
Elysian by performing dogs and wooden horses; between whiles
filtering (a few) through the gloomy Cathedral of Our Lady to say a
word or two at the base of a pillar within flare of a rusty little
gridiron-full of gusty little tapers; without the walls encompassing
Paris with dancing, love-making, wine-drinking, tobacco-smoking,
tomb-visiting, billiard card and domino playing, quack-doctoring, and
much murderous refuse, animate and inanimate—only last Sunday, my
Lady, in the desolation of Boredom and the clutch of Giant Despair,
almost hated her own maid for being in spirits.

I looked at her, but I could not see her, I could not hear her, I
could not draw my breath. The beating of my heart was so violent and
wild that I felt as if my life were breaking from me. But when she
caught me to her breast, kissed me, wept over me, compassionated me,
and called me back to myself; when she fell down on her knees and
cried to me, “Oh, my child, my child, I am your wicked and unhappy
mother! Oh, try to forgive me!”—when I saw her at my feet on the
bare earth in her great agony of mind, I felt, through all my tumult
of emotion, a burst of gratitude to the providence of God that I was
so changed as that I never could disgrace her by any trace of
likeness, as that nobody could ever now look at me and look at her
and remotely think of any near tie between us.

c48:p128.text:
A very quiet night. When the moon shines very brilliantly, a solitude
and stillness seem to proceed from her that influence even crowded
places full of life. Not only is it a still night on dusty high roads
and on hill-summits, whence a wide expanse of country may be seen in
repose, quieter and quieter as it spreads away into a fringe of trees
against the sky with the grey ghost of a bloom upon them; not only is
it a still night in gardens and in woods, and on the river where the
water-meadows are fresh and green, and the stream sparkles on among
pleasant islands, murmuring weirs, and whispering rushes; not only
does the stillness attend it as it flows where houses cluster thick,
where many bridges are reflected in it, where wharves and shipping
make it black and awful, where it winds from these disfigurements
through marshes whose grim beacons stand like skeletons washed
ashore, where it expands through the bolder region of rising grounds,
rich in cornfield wind-mill and steeple, and where it mingles with
the ever-heaving sea; not only is it a still night on the deep, and
on the shore where the watcher stands to see the ship with her spread
wings cross the path of light that appears to be presented to only
him; but even on this stranger’s wilderness of London there is some
rest. Its steeples and towers and its one great dome grow more
ethereal; its smoky house-tops lose their grossness in the pale
effulgence; the noises that arise from the streets are fewer and are
softened, and the footsteps on the pavements pass more tranquilly
away. In these fields of Mr. Tulkinghorn’s inhabiting, where the
shepherds play on Chancery pipes that have no stop, and keep their
sheep in the fold by hook and by crook until they have shorn them
exceeding close, every noise is merged, this moonlight night, into a
distant ringing hum, as if the city were a vast glass, vibrating.
c48:p128.summary: The narrator provides an extended, elaborate description of moonlit calm across the natural world, from countryside to ocean, ending with Chancery metaphors for Tulkinghorn's world.
c48:p128.best_quote: In these fields of Mr. Tulkinghorn's inhabiting, where the shepherds play on Chancery pipes that have no stop, and keep their sheep in the fold by hook and by crook until they have shorn them exceeding close, every noise is merged, this moonlight night, into a distant ringing hum, as if the city were a vast glass, vibrating.

c51:p27.text:
“Nor I,” said Richard moodily. “Who ever did?” He brightened again in
a moment and said with his natural openness, “Woodcourt, I should be
sorry to be misunderstood by you, even if I gained by it in your
estimation. You must know that I have done no good this long time. I
have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of
nothing else. It may be that I should have done better by keeping out
of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not,
though I dare say you will soon hear, if you have not already heard,
a very different opinion. To make short of a long story, I am afraid
I have wanted an object; but I have an object now—or it has me—and
it is too late to discuss it. Take me as I am, and make the best of
me.”
c51:p27.summary: Richard confesses to Woodcourt that he has accomplished nothing, lacks purpose, and feels trapped by fate and the Chancery suit, yet demands acceptance without judgment.

cP:p2.text:
But as it is wholesome that the parsimonious public should know what
has been doing, and still is doing, in this connexion, I mention here
that everything set forth in these pages concerning the Court of
Chancery is substantially true, and within the truth. The case of
Gridley is in no essential altered from one of actual occurrence,
made public by a disinterested person who was professionally
acquainted with the whole of the monstrous wrong from beginning to
end. At the present moment (August, 1853) there is a suit before the
court which was commenced nearly twenty years ago, in which from
thirty to forty counsel have been known to appear at one time, in
which costs have been incurred to the amount of seventy thousand
pounds, which is A FRIENDLY SUIT, and which is (I am assured) no
nearer to its termination now than when it was begun. There is
another well-known suit in Chancery, not yet decided, which was
commenced before the close of the last century and in which more than
double the amount of seventy thousand pounds has been swallowed up in
costs. If I wanted other authorities for Jarndyce and Jarndyce, I
could rain them on these pages, to the shame of—a parsimonious
public.
cP:p2.summary: Dickens asserts the factual basis of his Chancery depictions by citing real cases: a twenty-year suit with seventy thousand pounds in costs and another century-old suit with double that amount.
cP:p2.best_quote: If I wanted other authorities for Jarndyce and Jarndyce, I could rain them on these pages, to the shame of—a parsimonious public.

c15:p107.text:
“Mr. Jarndyce,” said Gridley with a rough sort of salutation, “you
bear your wrongs more quietly than I can bear mine. More than that, I
tell you—and I tell this gentleman, and these young ladies, if they
are friends of yours—that if I took my wrongs in any other way, I
should be driven mad! It is only by resenting them, and by revenging
them in my mind, and by angrily demanding the justice I never get,
that I am able to keep my wits together. It is only that!” he said,
speaking in a homely, rustic way and with great vehemence. “You may
tell me that I over-excite myself. I answer that it’s in my nature to
do it, under wrong, and I must do it. There’s nothing between doing
it, and sinking into the smiling state of the poor little mad woman
that haunts the court. If I was once to sit down under it, I should
become imbecile.”
c15:p107.summary: Gridley explains that his rage is essential to his sanity; without the outlet of resenting and avenging his wrongs in thought, he would become imbecile like 'the poor little mad woman that haunts the court.'
c15:p107.best_quote: if I took my wrongs in any other way, I should be driven mad! It is only by resenting them, and by revenging them in my mind, and by angrily demanding the justice I never get, that I am able to keep my wits together.

c15:p44.text:

the same angry stare on each in succession as they passed and
followed me. Mr. Jarndyce gave him good day. “Good day!” he said
abruptly and fiercely. He was a tall, sallow man with a careworn head
on which but little hair remained, a deeply lined face, and prominent
eyes. He had a combative look and a chafing, irritable manner which,
associated with his figure—still large and powerful, though
evidently in its decline—rather alarmed me. He had a pen in his
hand, and in the glimpse I caught of his room in passing, I saw that
it was covered with a litter of papers.

c44:p33.text:
It was not a love letter, though it expressed so much love, but was
written just as he would at any time have spoken to me. I saw his
face, and heard his voice, and felt the influence of his kind
protecting manner in every line. It addressed me as if our places
were reversed, as if all the good deeds had been mine and all the
feelings they had awakened his. It dwelt on my being young, and he
past the prime of life; on his having attained a ripe age, while I
was a child; on his writing to me with a silvered head, and knowing
all this so well as to set it in full before me for mature
deliberation. It told me that I would gain nothing by such a marriage
and lose nothing by rejecting it, for no new relation could enhance
the tenderness in which he held me, and whatever my decision was, he
was certain it would be right. But he had considered this step anew
since our late confidence and had decided on taking it, if it only
served to show me through one poor instance that the whole world
would readily unite to falsify the stern prediction of my childhood.
I was the last to know what happiness I could bestow upon him, but of
that he said no more, for I was always to remember that I owed him
nothing and that he was my debtor, and for very much. He had often
thought of our future, and foreseeing that the time must come, and
fearing that it might come soon, when Ada (now very nearly of age)
would leave us, and when our present mode of life must be broken up,
had become accustomed to reflect on this proposal. Thus he made it.
If I felt that I could ever give him the best right he could have to
be my protector, and if I felt that I could happily and justly become
the dear companion of his remaining life, superior to all lighter
chances and changes than death, even then he could not have me bind
myself irrevocably while this letter was yet so new to me, but even
then I must have ample time for reconsideration. In that case, or in
the opposite case, let him be unchanged in his old relation, in his
old manner, in the old name by which I called him. And as to his
bright Dame Durden and little housekeeper, she would ever be the
same, he knew.
c44:p33.summary: Esther recounts the substance of Jarndyce's letter: it is written with selfless love and deference; he emphasizes her youth versus his age, her disfigurement versus his devotion, that she owes him nothing, and that if she accepts, he asks only that she reconsider with time and remain as she is.
c44:p33.best_quote: It addressed me as if our places were reversed, as if all the good deeds had been mine and all the feelings they had awakened his.

c5:p56.text:
“Aye!” said the old man, coming slowly out of his abstraction. “Yes!
Tom Jarndyce—you’ll excuse me, being related; but he was never known
about court by any other name, and was as well known there as—she is
now,” nodding slightly at his lodger. “Tom Jarndyce was often in
here. He got into a restless habit of strolling about when the cause
was on, or expected, talking to the little shopkeepers and telling
’em to keep out of Chancery, whatever they did. ‘For,’ says he, ‘it’s
being ground to bits in a slow mill; it’s being roasted at a slow
fire; it’s being stung to death by single bees; it’s being drowned by
drops; it’s going mad by grains.’ He was as near making away with
himself, just where the young lady stands, as near could be.”

c5:p58.text:
“He come in at the door,” said the old man, slowly pointing an
imaginary track along the shop, “on the day he did it—the whole
neighbourhood had said for months before that he would do it, of a
certainty sooner or later—he come in at the door that day, and
walked along there, and sat himself on a bench that stood there, and
asked me (you’ll judge I was a mortal sight younger then) to fetch
him a pint of wine. ‘For,’ says he, ‘Krook, I am much depressed; my
cause is on again, and I think I’m nearer judgment than I ever was.’
I hadn’t a mind to leave him alone; and I persuaded him to go to the
tavern over the way there, t’other side my lane (I mean Chancery
Lane); and I followed and looked in at the window, and saw him,
comfortable as I thought, in the arm-chair by the fire, and company
with him. I hadn’t hardly got back here when I heard a shot go
echoing and rattling right away into the inn. I ran out—neighbours
ran out—twenty of us cried at once, ‘Tom Jarndyce!’”
c5:p58.summary: Krook describes in vivid detail Tom Jarndyce's final day: how he came into the shop depressed, asked for wine, was persuaded to go to a tavern, and then shot himself. The neighbourhood had long predicted this tragedy.
c5:p58.best_quote: For, says he, Krook, I am much depressed; my cause is on again, and I think I'm nearer judgment than I ever was.

and treated her with great kindness, and kept her always near her.
Now this lady preserved a secret under all her greatness, which she
had preserved for many years. In fact, she had in early life been
engaged to marry a young rake—he was a captain in the army—nothing
connected with whom came to any good. She never did marry him, but
she gave birth to a child of which he was the father.”

c40:p96.text:
“The captain in the army being dead, she believed herself safe; but a
train of circumstances with which I need not trouble you led to
discovery. As I received the story, they began in an imprudence on
her own part one day when she was taken by surprise, which shows how
difficult it is for the firmest of us (she was very firm) to be
always guarded. There was great domestic trouble and amazement, you
may suppose; I leave you to imagine, Sir Leicester, the husband’s
grief. But that is not the present point. When Mr. Rouncewell’s
townsman heard of the disclosure, he no more allowed the girl to be
patronized and honoured than he would have suffered her to be trodden
underfoot before his eyes. Such was his pride, that he indignantly
took her away, as if from reproach and disgrace. He had no sense of
the honour done him and his daughter by the lady’s condescension; not
the least. He resented the girl’s position, as if the lady had been
the commonest of commoners. That is the story. I hope Lady Dedlock
will excuse its painful nature.”
